native_result.query: At what Socioeconomic levels is the advantage in completion rates for Black students more pronounced?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students becomes more pronounced at higher SES levels indicated by a positive interaction term SES*is_Black(coefficient:0.6271 (significant))
native_result.HypoB: The advantage in BA completion rates for Black students relative to White students is concentrated at the very top of the socioeconomic status distribution. At the highest SES decile (SES > 0.95), Black students' completion rate (6.1%) exceeds that of White students (4.9%), reversing the pattern observed at all nine lower deciles where Black completion rates are consistently lower (gaps from −0.004 to −0.036). This top-of-distribution advantage is a point-estimate pattern in unadjusted rates (Fisher p=0.59, 5 Black completions) but becomes statistically significant after adjusting for ability and sex (adjusted OR=3.09, 95% CI [1.13, 8.51], p=0.029). The advantage is absent or reversed at all lower SES levels: at the top tertile (a coarser bin), the Black-White gap remains negative (−0.016), and with fixed bins the gap turns positive only above SES ≈ 0.5 and sharply above SES ≈ 2.0. Black students at the highest SES level complete at higher rates than White students despite having lower measured ability (ASVAB composite gap of −246 points at D10), suggesting that socioeconomic resources at the top of the distribution may partially offset the ability disadvantage for Black students.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1. Loaded and inspected data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows, 0 missing). 2. Created SES deciles (quantile bins) and computed unadjusted Black vs White completion rates within each decile using BA DEGREE COMPLETED as the outcome. 3. Identified the decile(s) where the Black-minus-White gap is positive. 4. Ran sensitivity checks: (a) SES tertiles, (b) fixed SES bins at 0.5-unit intervals, (c) logistic regression with Black×SES_decile interactions adjusted for ability composite (z-scored) and sex. 5. Computed ability and class-percentile gaps by decile for context. 6. Formulated the hypothesis based on the convergence of findings across all analyses.
